nodes.name: Turtle grass
nodes.desc: Seagrass meadows shelter young fish and many small invertebrates. Turtles, parrotfish and sea urchins graze them, and dead leaves become detritus.

nodes.name: Green macroalgae
nodes.desc: Calcified green algae on sand flats and reefs, grazed by conch, turtles and parrotfish.

nodes.name: Red mangrove
nodes.desc: Mangroves cover much of the park. Their prop roots shelter young reef animals such as juvenile spiny lobsters before they move to the reef.

nodes.name: Pigeon berry
nodes.desc: A coastal scrub shrub with fruit. GloBI records show white-crowned pigeons eating its fruit.

nodes.name: Bahamian hutia
nodes.desc: A mostly plant-eating rodent that was introduced to the park in 1973 as a conservation measure. It eats leaves, shoots, fruit and bark.

nodes.name: Northern Bahamian rock iguana
nodes.desc: A mostly plant-eating lizard of coastal scrub and beaches. The Exuma population is threatened by feral animals and development.

nodes.name: White-crowned pigeon
nodes.desc: A fruit-eating pigeon, one of the best-recorded birds near the park. GloBI records link it to pigeon berry fruit.

nodes.name: Queen conch
nodes.desc: A snail that browses algae and seagrass in meadows. Overfishing is a concern in the Bahamas, and the park is a no-fishing zone.

nodes.name: Stoplight parrotfish
nodes.desc: Scrapes algae from dead coral. It is very important on Caribbean reefs because of how abundant it is.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: Adults mostly graze seagrass and algae in shallow lagoons and bays. Juveniles also eat animals.

nodes.name: Caribbean spiny lobster
nodes.desc: Eats mollusks, crustaceans, worms and dead animals. Juveniles settle among algae, seagrass and mangrove roots.

nodes.name: Nassau grouper
nodes.desc: A reef predator of fish and small crustaceans. Spawning gatherings make it easy to overfish, and it is critically endangered.

nodes.name: Red lionfish
nodes.desc: An invasive predator of small fish and crustaceans, established across the Bahamas. Few predators are known to eat it.

nodes.name: Osprey
nodes.desc: A fish-eating raptor, the only animal allowed to fish in the park.

nodes.name: Caribbean reef shark
nodes.desc: One of the largest reef predators. It eats reef fish, cephalopods and rays, and is protected in the Bahamas.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: A large shark that preys on adult green turtles, among other prey.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong sun on clear, shallow water powers seagrass, algae and mangroves.

nodes.name: Tides and currents
nodes.desc: Tides flush the mangroves and shallow banks, carrying nutrients and larvae.

nodes.name: Thin limestone soil
nodes.desc: Shallow, sandy soil over limestone supports low coastal scrub.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, algae, leaf litter and carcasses into nutrients.
